transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How can I help you today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. For the past few years I feel worn out all the time, like I’m running on empty even when I’m not doing that much. It just seems like no matter what I do, I can't shake this constant exhaustion.
Do you notice that your muscles feel weak, especially after activity, or does the tiredness mostly affect your energy and mood?

It's not really a physical muscle weakness from being active, but more of a constant, heavy lack of energy. Even on days when I barely leave my desk, my body feels like it's filled with sand, and this exhaustion just leaves me feeling completely gray, joyless, and running on empty.
Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, or do you still find pleasure in things like hobbies, socializing, or favorite pastimes?

Yes, I really have. Everything feels gray and joyless now, and I’ve stopped doing things I used to love like painting, weekend hikes, and photographing the Temecula hills. I also find myself bowing out of social plans and don't even have the energy to return my friends' texts anymore.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt little or no pleasure in activities you once enjoyed, even when you make an effort to do them?

Yes, but it's actually been much longer than two weeks—I've felt this way steadily for the past few years. Even when I make the effort to do things like paint, photograph the hills, or go on vacations, it all feels completely joyless and gray. My husband has even pointed out that I don't seem to take any pleasure in planning our outings anymore.
Have you had these symptoms of low mood and loss of interest nearly every day for most of the day, and have they persisted for at least two years or more?

Yes, absolutely. It has been pretty much every single day for a little over three years now, ever since my company went through a major restructuring. It just feels like a steady, heavy cloud has been hanging over me this entire time without ever really lifting.

F32.1 typically applies to episodic depressive episodes lasting at least two weeks but not exceeding two years in duration without remission, which does not fit this chronic course. Therefore, the current candidate has shifted from F32.1 to F34.1 (persistent depressive disorder, dysthymia) to better reflect the long-standing, continuous nature of the patient’s symptoms.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a chronic, dysthymic mood disturbance characterized by persistent low energy, anhedonia, and loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, occurring nearly every day for over three years, with associated functional impairment in social and personal domains. The duration and quality of symptoms align with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), rather than a major depressive episode, which would typically have more severe or episodic features.
